title: Optimizing Analytic Constants via AI-Guided Lean Proof Refinement
claim: A human-seeded structured artifact is refined by an iterative agent loop into an improved, verified artifact with the same dependency structure.
layout: 3 panels, left-to-right, central cycle loop between input and output graphs
description: A left-to-right three-part diagram. On the left, a small proof blueprint graph shows two blue 'axioms' nodes pointing into an orange 'editable subgoal' node, which points to a green 'proof goal' node. A bold arrow leads to a large light-blue rounded box titled 'AI Proof-Refinement Agent'. Inside, a clockwise cycle links three dashed boxes: a peach Planner, a green Generator and a pink Evaluator, each with a small icon. Italic gray notes sit beside the arrows: 'Run experiments / Propose approach / Generate contract', 'Refine Lean code', and 'Compile proof / Certify numerics / Score candidate'. Another arrow leads to the right-hand 'Refined Proof Blueprint', the same graph with the subgoal and goal nodes outlined in thick orange and green. The eye goes first to the central blue agent loop.
caption: AI-guided proof refinement. A human-seeded proof blueprint exposes editable lemmas and numerical certificates. An AI agent proposes local edits, the verifier checks Lean obligations and interval arithmetic certificates, and the result is fed back as the optimization signal.
abstract: AI agents are increasingly capable of discovering new mathematical results, yet their reasoning and generated proofs can be difficult to understand and verify. We introduce an interpretable framework for AI-guided mathematical discovery, focused on improving quantitative bounds on analytic constants. Our key insight is that existing proofs often contain slack in intermediate lemmas, which can be tightened without reconstructing the entire argument. To exploit this structure, we represent proofs as partially-formalized Lean blueprints: human-interpretable dependency graphs of definitions, lemmas, and theorems. An AI agent then iteratively refines the Lean code while preserving the blueprint's dependency structure, allowing local improvements to automatically propagate to a verified final bound. This interpretable structure allows humans to inspect the agent's refinements and understand how local improvements propagate to the final theorem. For Grothendieck's constant, we obtain $$ \mathcal{K}_G \leq \frac{\pi}{2\log(1+\sqrt{2})} - 10^{-17}, $$ the first explicit numerical improvement at the time over Krivine's 1977 bound. For Korenblum's constant, we obtain $$ \mathcal{K}_K \geq 0.356565, $$ improving Wang's 2025 bound of $0.3554$. Our experiments demonstrate the potential of both partial formalization and iterative agentic refinement for interpretable mathematical discovery.
